text:
I will estimate the causal effect of log household income on recent illness using the 1993 random village draw as an exogenous shock: implement a panel difference‑in‑differences and two‑stage least squares (2SLS) estimation that first uses transfer_draw (village drawn into the unconditional quarterly cash transfer) to instrument log household income and then estimates the effect on the number of reported illness episodes, including individual and survey‑round fixed effects and clustering SEs at the village level. Key variables are outcome = illness episodes in the last four weeks, endogenous treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, instrument = transfer_draw (restrict sample to the 6 pilot‑area villages where the draw occurred and use pre/post rounds), and controls for time‑varying covariates (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic) to improve precision and check parallel trends; I will also report the reduced‑form ITT. I will pre‑test parallel trends using pre‑draw rounds and present weak‑instrument‑robust inference (Anderson‑Rubin/CIS and cluster‑robust IV), and I will supplement IV with the reduced‑form DiD estimate to show local average treatment effects and intent‑to‑treat. The main threat is the very weak first stage (reported F≈2) and the small number of treated clusters, which limits power and makes IV estimates imprecise and sensitive to cluster‑level departures from randomization or spillovers. I will therefore treat transfer_draw as a plausibly exogenous instrument but rely primarily on the reduced‑form DiD and weak‑instrument‑robust confidence sets for inference.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will identify the causal effect by instrumental-variables estimation (2SLS) in a person-panel with individual and survey-round fixed effects, using the randomized village draw for the unconditional cash transfer (transfer_draw) as an instrument for log household income per adult equivalent and also reporting the reduced-form; standard errors will be clustered at the village level. Key variables are treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, outcome = number of illness episodes in the four weeks before interview, instrument = transfer_draw, and covariates/fixed effects including hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic, education, age, gender and survey-round indicators to absorb common shocks. I will pre-test instrument balance on baseline covariates and report first-stage diagnostics, and because transfer_draw is defined only within the 6 pilot-area villages I will present both the IV LATE and the reduced-form/ITT estimates for transparency. The main threat is a weak first stage (first-stage F ≈ 2) and limited external validity from estimating effects only in the small pilot sample; I will therefore report weak-IV-robust CIs (Anderson–Rubin), present sensitivity bounds, and contrast with supplementary analyses using season_rain while noting its likely exclusion restriction violations. 

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | doubtful
season_rain | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect by instrumenting log household income per adult equivalent with assignment to the 1993 cash‑transfer draw (transfer_draw, interacted with a post‑draw indicator) and estimating 2SLS in the individual panel so identification comes from the randomized village draw. The endogenous regressor is log household income per adult equivalent, the outcome is number of illness episodes in the four weeks before interview, and I will include individual and survey‑round fixed effects plus baseline covariates (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic, land_acres). Because the draw affects income only at the village level, I will cluster standard errors at the village level and report weak‑instrument–robust inference (first‑stage F, Anderson–Rubin or LIML) given the reported first‑stage F≈2. I will restrict primary analysis to the pilot villages (or run a DID‑IV using all observations where transfer_draw is nonmissing) to avoid misclassification of assignment, and I will use individual fixed effects to control for time‑invariant household heterogeneity. The main threat is the very weak first stage and the small number of clusters (imprecision and finite‑sample IV bias), plus potential spillovers or differential post‑draw trends in drawn villages that could violate the exclusion restriction. I will therefore present OLS and IV side‑by‑side, run placebo/pre‑trend checks, and report weak‑instrument robust CIs and sensitivity analyses excluding neighboring villages.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares in the panel: instrument log household income per adult equivalent with exogenous seasonal rainfall shocks interacted with household land holdings (season_rain * land_acres), and include individual and survey‑round fixed effects (cluster SEs at the village) so identification comes from differential income responses to the same rainfall shock across households with different land exposure. Key variables are the treatment log household income per adult equivalent, the outcome number of self‑reported illness episodes in the prior four weeks, and the instrument season_rain * land_acres (season_rain is the deviation from long‑run average; land_acres is baseline acres farmed). The interaction isolates income variation driven by crop returns (relevance) while fixed effects absorb time‑invariant household heterogeneity and common time shocks. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction because rainfall can directly affect health (e.g., vector‑borne disease incidence and the regional suspension of mobile clinics after wet seasons) or because land_acres may correlate with unobserved location‑specific health risks; I will report first‑stage F‑statistics, placebo tests on non‑farmers, estimates excluding wet‑season rounds, and sensitivity analyses including the randomized transfer_draw as a secondary instrument where applicable. I also consider raw season_rain (directly likely violates exclusion) and transfer_draw (randomized but weak and limited to 6 villages) as alternative instruments and will present OLS, IV, and robustness checks together to assess credibility. 

CANDIDATES:
season_rain | violated
transfer_draw | doubtful
season_rain*land_acres | plausible
INSTRUMENT: season_rain*land_acres

I'll identify causal effect with an instrumental-variables difference-in-differences: use the 1993 randomized village draw for the fund (transfer_draw interacted with a post-draw indicator) as an instrument for log household income per adult equivalent and estimate its effect on the number of self-reported illness episodes in the prior four weeks. I will restrict the main sample to households in the six pilot-area villages (pre- and post-draw rounds) and estimate two-stage least squares with individual (person) and survey-round fixed effects, clustering standard errors at the village level. Key variables are outcome = illness episodes (count), treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, instrument = transfer_draw × post indicator; include time-varying controls (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic, land_acres) and report IV first-stage statistics. Because the first-stage is weak in the full release (first-stage F ≈ 2), I will report weak-IV-robust confidence intervals (Anderson–Rubin), present the reduced-form (ITT) estimates, and run Poisson fixed-effects and OLS FE robustness checks. The main threat is a weak instrument and small pilot-area sample raising imprecision and limited external validity, plus possible spillovers or compositional changes (migration or reporting) after the draw; I will therefore present bounds and sensitivity checks rather than rely only on point estimates. I will not use season_rain as an instrument because it plausibly violates the exclusion restriction (it affects clinic rounds and direct access to care).

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect by two-stage least squares using the 1993 randomized selection into the fund’s pilot as the instrument: specifically, assignment to a drawn village (transfer_draw) interacted with a post-1993 indicator will instrument log household income per adult equivalent, and the second stage will regress the number of self-reported illness episodes in the prior four weeks on the instrumented income. I will restrict the main analysis to the 6-village pilot area (where transfer_draw is observed), include individual fixed effects and survey-round fixed effects to absorb time-invariant confounders and common shocks, and add baseline controls (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic) and cluster standard errors at the village level. Because the documented first-stage is weak (F ≈ 2) I will report LATE estimates and use weak-IV-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin and LIML) and present reduced-form estimates as well. I will test pre-draw balance and parallel trends in outcomes and income, control for season_rain to reduce correlated weather shocks, and perform sensitivity checks for spillovers and heterogeneous effects. The main threat is a weak instrument (imprecise/biased finite-sample IV) plus limited external validity (only 6 villages) and potential post-draw differential trends or spillovers that violate exclusion. CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate a local average treatment effect (LATE) using two-stage least squares where the endogenous treatment is an indicator for graduating high school by age 19 and the outcome is an indicator for having voted in at least one general election 1998–2008 from the voter files; the instrument is the district's randomized elective-credit waiver (credit_waiver), which was randomly assigned in the 1965 senior draw and increased graduation by ~4 percentage points while the program memo reports it "changed nothing else." Key variables are: instrument = credit_waiver (restricted to the 1965-wave students who reached 12th grade), endogenous regressor = graduated_by_19, outcome = voted_1998_2008, plus baseline covariates (female, birth_year, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index) only to improve precision. I will report first-stage statistics and use weak-instrument-robust inference (e.g., Anderson–Rubin/conditional likelihood ratio) because the first-stage F≈2 suggests a weak instrument, and I will interpret estimates as LATE for compliers in the 1965 senior subgroup. The main threat is weak instrument strength and limited external validity due to the instrument applying to a small, selected subgroup (only 1965 seniors who reached 12th grade), and any undetected violations of the exclusion restriction (if the waiver affected unobserved behaviors other than graduation). As robustness checks I will (a) compare OLS and IV estimates, (b) run AR tests and report confidence sets, and (c) examine balance and pre-treatment outcomes in the 1965 cohort to probe the exclusion assumption.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect using instrumental variables (2SLS) exploiting the district's randomized 1965 elective-credit waiver as an instrument for graduating from high school by age 19, because program documentation states the waiver was randomly assigned within that senior class and “changed nothing else.” The key variables are: treatment = graduated_high_school_by19 (binary), instrument = credit_waiver, outcome = voted_in_any_general_1998_2008 (from public voter files), with baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, father_home) and cohort indicators included only to improve precision and adjust for any residual imbalance. Because the waiver applies only to the 1965 senior cohort I will restrict the IV sample to eligible students, report first-stage statistics (F-stat), use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin / LIML), and present the LATE interpretation for compliers. I will run balance tests of the instrument on pre-treatment covariates and placebo outcomes and report the reduced-form (ITT) alongside IV to show the effect of random assignment directly. The main remaining threat is a weak and imprecise instrument (reported first-stage F≈2) combined with small sample size and limited external validity—weak-instrument bias and wide CIs could make point estimates unreliable. If the waiver instrument is too weak I will prefer and transparently report reduced-form effects and sensitivity bounds rather than over-interpret noisy IV point estimates.

CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | violated
credit_waiver | plausible
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the local average treatment effect of graduating high school by age 19 on adult turnout using two-stage least squares (fuzzy IV) where the instrument is the district's randomized 1965 elective credit waiver that induced a modest increase in graduation. The outcome is the voter-file indicator for voting in at least one general election 1998–2008, the treatment is an indicator for graduated from high school by age 19, and the instrument is credit_waiver; I will restrict the main IV sample to the 1965 cohort and include baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year, father_home) for precision. I will report weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin/CAR scores and LIML), present first-stage diagnostics, and conduct sensitivity checks including reduced-form and intent-to-treat estimates in the full sample. The main remaining threat is a weak first stage (documented F ≈ 2) that undermines precision and identification and limits external validity to the 1965 wave; secondary threats are any unrecorded cohort-specific violations of the exclusion restriction or differential measurement/matching to the voter file. 
CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | doubtful
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate a fuzzy IV (2SLS) LATE of graduating high school by 19 on voting using randomized assignment to the two‑year half‑day preschool program as the instrument (first stage: graduated_by19 ~ preschool_assign; second stage: voted_1998_2008 ~ predicted_graduated_by19). Key variables are preschool_assign (instrument), graduated_by19 (treatment), voted_1998_2008 (binary outcome), and baseline covariates female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, father_home, birth_year and wave dummies to improve precision and to check balance. I will report the reduced form (ITT) of preschool_assign on voting as the most credible randomized estimate and use credit_waiver in the 1965 subsample as an alternative instrument only for sensitivity (it has a weak first stage). The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction: the preschool arm included a civic club that took children to the polls with parents (a plausible direct path from preschool_assign to adult voting), and the 1965 credit waiver is weak and cohort‑limited, so IV estimates may be biased or imprecise; if so I will rely on ITT, mediation, and bounding instead.  

CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | violated
credit_waiver | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: NONE

I will estimate the causal effect of graduating high school by age 19 on adult turnout using instrumental variables (2SLS) with the district's randomized elective-credit waiver (credit_waiver) as the instrument, restricting the sample to the 1965 senior-wave students who reached 12th grade so the first-stage is defined; this gives a LATE for compliers. Key variables are the binary outcome "voted at least once 1998–2008", the endogenous binary treatment "graduated by 19", the instrument "credit_waiver", and baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, father_home, birth_year) for precision and balance checks. I will report first-stage statistics and use weak-IV–robust inference (Anderson–Rubin, LIML, robust CIs) and present ITT and reduced-form estimates alongside 2SLS to transparently show strength and effect heterogeneity. The main threat is that the instrument is weak (first-stage F≈2) and identified LATE applies to a small, selected subsample (limited external validity); a secondary concern is any unmeasured channel by which the waiver could have affected turnout other than via graduation. As robustness I will (a) bound effects, (b) run placebo outcomes and balance tests, and (c) report intent-to-treat turnout differences from the preschool random assignment only as descriptive ITT evidence because preschool_assign included civic-club poll exposure likely violating IV exclusion.  

CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | violated
credit_waiver | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate a local causal effect using instrumental variables (Wald/2SLS) exploiting the randomized credit_waiver draw in the 1965 senior cohort as an instrument for graduating from high school by age 19, restricting the IV sample to the subgroup for whom the waiver is defined (1965 students who reached 12th grade). Key variables are the binary treatment graduated_by19, the binary outcome voted1998_2008 from public voter files, the instrument credit_waiver, and baseline covariates (birth_year, female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index) included to improve precision and for balance checks. I will report first-stage statistics (F-stat, compliance share), the IV LATE estimate with robust standard errors, weak-instrument-robust confidence intervals (e.g., Anderson–Rubin), and the reduced-form/ITT for transparency. Main threats are a weak instrument (first-stage F≈2) that yields imprecise and potentially unreliable IV estimates and limited external validity of the LATE, plus any violation of the exclusion restriction if the waiver affected turnout through channels other than graduation. As a robustness exercise I will present reduced-form estimates in the full sample and an IV using preschool_assign only as a sensitivity check while explicitly flagging that preschool_assign likely violates exclusion because program children were taken to the polls via a civic club.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect of segregation on per-capita direct general expenditure by two-stage least squares, using the randomized 1990 fair‑housing audit grant (audit_grant) as an instrument for the city entropy segregation index, exploiting the panel nature (1980–2010) with state-by-year fixed effects and controls for log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, and own_rate to absorb time and compositional confounders. The first stage predicts segregation with audit_grant (restricted to the subsample with non-missing grant data) and the second stage regresses expenditure per resident on the predicted segregation, clustering standard errors at an appropriate level; because the published first-stage F≈2 suggests weakness, I will report LIML and Anderson–Rubin confidence sets in addition to 2SLS. Key variables are: treatment = multigroup entropy segregation index, outcome = direct general expenditure per resident, instrument = audit_grant, and covariates = log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate plus state-by-year fixed effects. The main threat is a weak instrument and limited external validity (the grant applies to a small subset of large cities), plus the possibility that the grant influenced municipal spending through other channels (NGO mobilization or political pressure) violating exclusion; I will test balance on pre‑grant covariates and present sensitivity/robustness checks. If the IV is unusably weak, I will present reduced‑form estimates and difference‑in‑differences-style event plots for the grant subsample as a complementary analysis.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | violated
audit_grant | plausible
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will estimate the causal effect with two-stage least squares (2SLS) in a panel with city fixed effects and state-by-year fixed effects, instrumenting the city segregation entropy index with the randomized fair‑housing audit grant (audit_grant) drawn among 40 eligible large cities. Key variables are the treatment segregation index, the outcome direct general expenditure per resident, and controls log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate and region, with SEs clustered at the city level. The audit_grant is plausibly exogenous in the eligible subsample because it was randomly assigned and paid a nonprofit (not the city), and the PI notes it “changed nothing else,” but the first stage is weak (first-stage F≈2). I will therefore use weak‑instrument‑robust inference (Anderson‑Rubin and LIML), report reduced‑form and OLS alongside IV, and run balance tests and placebo outcomes to probe exclusion. As a robustness check I will explore waterways as an alternative instrument in sensitivity analyses but treat it as invalid for the main IV because state law requires flood‑control levies on boundary streams that plausibly affect municipal spending directly. The main remaining threat is limited external validity and imprecision from the small, instrument‑eligible subsample and any unobserved channels by which the grant or associated nonprofit activity might have affected city spending.

CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | plausible
waterways | violated
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares (2SLS) exploiting the 1990 randomized fair‑housing audit grant as an instrument for city racial segregation, restricting to the subsample where audit_grant is observed (the 40 cities >100,000 in the two participating states) and pooling census years with city fixed effects. Key variables: treatment = multigroup entropy segregation index (0–100), outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (dollars), instrument = audit_grant (random draw indicator), controls and adjustments = city fixed effects, state‑by‑year fixed effects, log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, and clustered SEs at the city level. Identification relies on random assignment of the grant affecting later segregation but (per documentation) not directly changing municipal budgets except through segregation; I will report first‑stage strength, use weak‑IV robust inference if needed, and check balance on pre‑treatment covariates. Main threat: the instrument is weak (first‑stage F ≈ 2) and the causal estimate will have limited external validity (only large cities in two states); there is also residual risk the audit program influenced spending via channels other than segregation despite the claim it “changed nothing else.” I will supplement IV with descriptive event‑study plots of segregation and spending around 1990 in the subsample to assess dynamics and pre‑trends.  
CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | plausible
waterways | violated
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will estimate causal effects with an instrumental-variables design using the randomized fair‑housing audit grant (audit_grant) as the instrument for the city's multigroup entropy segregation index, restricting the analysis to the 40 eligible cities originally in the random draw and including state-by-year fixed effects. The first stage will regress segregation (0–100) on audit_grant plus controls, and the second stage will regress direct general expenditure per resident (dollars) on the predicted segregation from the first stage. Key variables are: treatment = segregation index; outcome = direct general expenditure per resident; instrument = audit_grant; controls = log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, and state-by-year fixed effects; standard errors clustered at the city level. The exclusion restriction is plausible for the restricted sample because the grant paid a nonprofit to run audits (not city governments) and documentation says it changed nothing else. The principal threat is a weak first stage (documentation reports a first‑stage F ≈ 2), which yields imprecise and possibly biased IV estimates and limits power and external validity since identification comes from 40 large cities in two states. I will report first-stage diagnostics and weak‑instrument‑robust inference (e.g., Anderson–Rubin), and present sensitivity checks including OLS with rich controls and a geography-based instrument (waterways) only as a robustness check while noting its direct budgetary channel. 
CANDIDATES:
waterways | violated
audit_grant | plausible
region | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will estimate the causal effect of the city segregation index on direct general expenditure per resident using instrumental variables: exploiting the 1990 random draw that awarded a fair‑housing testing grant (audit_grant) as an instrument for later segregation in the subsample of large cities in the two participating states. Key variables are treatment = multigroup entropy segregation index, outcome = inflation‑adjusted direct general expenditure per resident, instrument = audit_grant, and controls = state-by-year fixed effects plus log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate and other time‑varying city covariates to improve precision. I will run two‑stage least squares on the eligible sample, cluster standard errors by city, and report first‑stage F‑statistics and weak‑IV robust confidence intervals, alongside OLS and reduced‑form estimates for transparency. The main threat is a weak instrument and limited external validity — the grant affects only ~40 large cities in two states and the reported first‑stage F≈2 makes IV estimates imprecise and sensitive to weak‑IV bias. A secondary threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the grant changed spending through channels other than segregation (e.g., nonprofit activity or political mobilization); I will test balance on pre‑grant covariates, estimate placebo outcomes, and present bounds and reduced‑form intent‑to‑treat results. If audit_grant proves unusable, I will report city fixed‑effects panel estimates with state‑by‑year trends as robustness checks.

CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | doubtful
waterways | violated
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will use an instrumental-variables design (2SLS) exploiting the 1990 federal fair‑housing testing grant random draw (audit_grant) as an exogenous shock to segregation, estimating the effect of the census-block entropy segregation index (0–100) on city direct general expenditure per resident while conditioning on state-by-year fixed effects and log population. In the first stage I will regress the segregation index on audit_grant and covariates; in the second stage I will regress per‑resident general expenditure on predicted segregation. Key variables are: treatment = segregation (entropy index), outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (real dollars), instrument = audit_grant, controls = log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, region, and fixed effects. The main threat is that audit_grant is available only for a small, nonrepresentative subset (40 large cities in two states) and has a weak first stage (F≈2), so IV estimates may be weak‑instrument biased and have limited external validity. To bolster credibility I will report OLS and IV side by side, use weak‑instrument‑robust inference (Anderson–Rubin), run placebo/pre‑trend tests on pre‑grant outcomes, and triangulate with sensitivity bounds; I will not use waterways as an instrument because state flood‑levy rules create a direct pathway to spending.

CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | doubtful
waterways | violated
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will identify the causal effect using instrumental variables (2SLS), exploiting the randomized county-level mailed reminder pilot (reminder_draw) as an instrument for turnout while including county and election-year fixed effects to absorb time-invariant county confounders and national shocks. Key variables are turnout (county percentage of voting-age population) as the endogenous treatment, incumbent-party vote share as the outcome, reminder_draw as the instrument, and dem_prev, pop_density, pct_rural, median_inc, and south as precision covariates. I will estimate the first-stage and report the F-statistic, use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin or LIML) and cluster standard errors at the county level. The sample will be restricted to the counties and election-years where reminder_draw is defined (the 180 county-elections in the 1996–2000 pilot), with balance tests and placebo checks on pre-treatment vote shares to assess exogeneity. The main threat is a weak instrument and limited external validity because the pilot is small (first-stage F ≈ 4) and there could be local spillovers or correlated campaign responses to the reminder despite its neutral wording.  

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: reminder_draw

I will estimate a local average treatment effect using two-stage least squares (2SLS), instrumenting county turnout (percent of voting-age population) with the randomized reminder_draw in the 1996–2000 pilot counties, and include county and election-year fixed effects plus baseline covariates (dem_prev, pop_density, pct_rural, median_inc, south) to improve precision. The outcome is incumbent-party county vote share (percentage points); the first stage uses reminder_draw to predict turnout within the pilot sample, and the second stage uses the fitted turnout to estimate its effect on vote share, clustering standard errors by county. This IV exploits randomized variation in turnout from the mailed, nonpartisan reminders (which named no candidate or party), so exclusion is plausibly satisfied insofar as the reminder affects the outcome only through turnout. I will report first-stage strength (F-statistic) and interpret results as the complier LATE; because the reminder raises turnout by only ~0.3 percentage points and the first-stage F ≈ 4, weak-instrument sensitivity (and limited external validity to nonpilot counties) is the main threat. As secondary checks I considered using election-day rainfall (eday_rain) as an instrument because it exogenously depressed turnout, but the 1952 law that moved polling places into courthouses with incumbent posters creates a direct pathway to votes and likely violates exclusion, so I will not use it as the main instrument.

CANDIDATES:
reminder_draw | plausible
eday_rain | violated
INSTRUMENT: reminder_draw

I will estimate the causal effect of turnout on the incumbent party's county vote share using two-stage least squares (2SLS) that exploits the randomized 1996–2000 mailed-reminder pilot: reminder_draw as an instrument for county turnout (percentage of VAP), with county and election-year fixed effects to absorb time-invariant county heterogeneity and common shocks. Key variables are treatment = county turnout (pct VAP), outcome = incumbent-party vote share (pct), instrument = reminder_draw (1 if county was randomly drawn to receive the mail reminder), and covariates for precision/balance checks such as dem_prev, pop_density, pct_rural, median_inc, and south. First stage: turnout_it = alpha + beta * reminder_draw_it + gamma * X_it + county_i + year_t + e_it; second stage: vote_share_it = alpha' + delta * fitted_turnout_it + gamma' * X_it + county_i + year_t + u_it; standard errors clustered by county and report weak-IV-robust (Anderson–Rubin) intervals given the modest first-stage (F≈4). I will pre-register and report balance tests for reminder_draw, show descriptive first-stage heterogeneity, and transparently report local-sample estimands and external-validity limits because reminder_draw exists only for 180 county-elections in three pilot states. The main threat is weak instrument precision and limited generalizability (and any deviation from the stated “changed nothing else” assumption in implementation), so I will complement IV estimates with intent-to-treat comparisons and sensitivity checks using alternative instruments. If reminder_draw is too weak or implementation violated, I will report reduced-form effects and interpret them as the randomized policy effect on turnout and vote share in the pilot sample.

CANDIDATES:
eday_rain | violated
reminder_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: reminder_draw

I will estimate the causal effect of turnout on incumbent-party county vote share by two-stage least squares using the randomized county-level mailed reminder (reminder_draw) as an instrument for turnout, with county and election-year fixed effects to absorb time-invariant county heterogeneity and common shocks. Key variables are: instrument = reminder_draw (1/0, observed for the 180 county‑elections in the three‑state 1996–2000 pilot), endogenous regressor = county turnout (percent of voting‑age population), outcome = incumbent-party vote share (percentage points); I will include dem_prev, pop_density, pct_rural, median_inc, south and state indicators as covariates and cluster SEs by county. Because the reminder was nonpartisan and named no candidate or party, exclusion is plausible, but the first-stage is weak (≈0.3 pp, F≈4) and the IV estimate will therefore be accompanied by weak‑instrument‑robust inference (AR, LIML) and bounds. I will restrict the primary IV sample to county‑elections with reminder_draw observed and report effects there (noting external‑validity limits), then run sensitivity checks using eday_rain as an alternative instrument, placebo tests on pre‑period vote shares, and Conley bounds for possible small violations of exclusion. The main remaining threat is a weak instrument combined with limited sample coverage and any systematic county‑level responses to reminders (campaign activity, registration drives) that would violate exclusion. If the reminder IV is too weak or shows signs of violation, I will report reduced‑form associations and bounds rather than rely on a single IV point estimate.

CANDIDATES:
reminder_draw | plausible
eday_rain | violated
INSTRUMENT: reminder_draw

I will estimate a local average treatment effect of turnout on incumbent-party vote share using two-stage least squares, instrumenting county turnout (percent of VAP) with the randomized reminder_draw in the 1996–2000 pilot and including county and election-year fixed effects with SEs clustered at the county level. The first stage is turnout_it = α + π·reminder_draw_it + X_itβ + μ_i + τ_t + ε_it and the second stage uses the fitted turnout to predict incumbent_party_share_it, with key covariates X including dem_prev, pop_density, pct_rural, median_inc, and south; I will also control for eday_rain to soak up weather shocks. I will restrict the IV analysis to the subset of county-elections with nonmissing reminder_draw (the three pilot states/years), report ITT, first-stage F, and LATE, and present reduced-form estimates and balance checks across drawn and undrawn counties. The main threat is weak instrument and limited external validity because only ~180 county-elections are randomized and the first-stage is modest (F ≈ 4), plus the possibility that the reminder changed voter composition or persuasion (violating exclusion). I will perform robustness checks using alternative specifications, permutation inference within the pilot, and a cautious discussion of generalizability.  
CANDIDATES:
reminder_draw | plausible
eday_rain | violated
INSTRUMENT: reminder_draw

I will identify the causal effect with two-stage least squares using the randomized county-level reminder_draw (the 1996–2000 mailed-reminder pilot) to instrument county turnout, estimating LATE with county and election-year fixed effects to remove time-invariant county confounders and common election shocks.
